newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - UK companies count cost of FX hedging policies.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UK companies count cost of FX hedging policies.

text.p: Britain's biggest companies have been pummelled by sterling's year-long surge, but many business executives remain wary of using hedging strategies involving derivatives such as options.
Some British executives said this bias could mean the damage to corporate bottom lines could persist even if the pound fell back, as many foreign exchange analysts now predict it will.

"The big D-word does frighten boards of companies because they are worried about unlimited losses and some just have a blanket rule about not getting involved with derivatives," said Angus Russell, group treasurer of the pharmaceuticals and chemicals company Zeneca Group Plc.

Exporters in the FTSE 100 have, for the most part, shied away from using options, which give them cover and leave them the freedom to sell their foreign-currency earnings at more lucrative rates in the spot market.
FORWARD BUYING CAN PROLONG PAIN OF STERLING STRENGTH

Instead, they have focused on using the forward market to fix rates at which they will buy pounds three to six months down the line. But because this is an ongoing process, which involves routinely buying forwards, the pain of sterling's rise could continue to be felt even if the spot goes into reverse.
With forwards, clients lock in rates in the knowledge they will forgo any potential benefit if the market moves their way.

With options, however, a company would pay a cost up front for the right to lock in at more favourable rates than the prevailing spot but it would also have the freedom to deal at the spot if it moves significantly in its favour.

"Used in the proper context, options can provide greater flexibility than forwards which lock you into a contract and might prove to be loss-making compared with the spot price on a given day," Russell said.
For Zeneca, this means setting a benchmark goal of hedging 50 percent of underlying currency exposure by buying options.
It can increase its bias towards forwards if it has a particularly firm view on an exchange rate, if currencies are especially stable or if a currency is moving in one direction.
"But in circumstances like the current environment where there is high volatility we use options to give flexibility," said Russell.
STERLING CAPPED FOR NOW BUT STILL SKY-HIGH

While sterling has pared gains from the eight-year highs it scaled last month against the mark, it is still more than 30 percent stronger than a year ago, and 50 pfennigs above many British exporters' ideal rate.
Its rise has been fuelled by rising interest rates and concern about the planned single European currency, but most traders agree that the pound has risen to unsustainable levels.
Concern is rife that the pound's strength will lead to a widening in Britain's trade deficit and that it could eventually tip the economy into a recession if allowed to persist.
Also, the quarter-percentage point increase in rates announced on Thursday may be the last rate rise in the cycle, analysts said.
FEAR OF HEDGING LIMITS OPTIONS
So why are companies locking themselves in with forwards at current levels?
Some, like lubricants maker Burmah Castrol, are unwilling to engage in any transactions which could be viewed as speculative.

"We hedge our known cash flows by buying forwards and hedge the balance sheet by keeping debt where our principal assets and earnings are," said James Alexander, corporate affairs director at Burmah Castrol.

"What we will not do, and what we regard as wrong, is to try to hedge the translation effect because we would be putting at risk shareholders' money for nothing but an accounting matter," he said. "This would be akin to speculation and not what shareholders are paying us for."

The translation effect of the pound's rise, or the erosion in the sterling value of British companies' overseas earnings, has also hit construction industry supplier RMC Group Plc. But it too is concentrating on forwards as a hedging tool.

"Our exports are negligible because we have extensive interests in Europe, particularly in Germany," said Robert Lambourne, the company's group finance director. "But the stock market's view of us is obviously influenced by the fact that our overseas earnings are being translated into sterling at a much lower rate now. We look at various things but we are relatively cautious and cover forward any transaction."
LOSS OF COMPETITIVENESS ADDS FURTHER PAIN
British manufacturers, meanwhile, have been hammered not only by the translation effects of sterling's rise but by the loss of competitiveness against rivals abroad.

"Manufacturing companies have both transaction and translation problems with sterling strength, but the dominant thing is the effect that the strength of sterling has on competitiveness," said Alan Armitage, head of economics at the Engineering Employers' Federation.
"The normal practice is for large manufacturing companies to hedge by covering forward but you can only hedge so far forward."
For instance, British Steel, 55 percent of whose sales are destined for overseas markets, saw its profits halved in the last fiscal year as a consequence of sterling's surge.

It is, however, sticking to its policy of selling and purchasing forward on a non-discretionary basis to hedge its transactions costs, it said. Much of this involves buying dollars and marks about six months forward, according to the company's press officer Mike Hitchcock.
HAUNTED BY MEMORIES OF PAST DISASTERS

Some of the British corporate caution stems from memories of disasters such as the one which befell Allied Lyons, the food and drinks conglomorate which lost 147 million pounds ($247.7 million) in 1991 writing currency options.
The only downside involved in buying options is the initial premium paid, and some say this cost can be considered non-speculative if the firm has an underlying exposure.
"The only loss is the premium cost of buying the option and there is no further downside loss given that we trade within the limits of our underlying existing exposure," said Russell at Zeneca.
This cost remains a deterrant.
"UK corporates are generally loath to pay the premium for options and prefer to stick to doing forwards," said a treasury economist at a British bank.
Moreover, the relative illiquidity of sterling markets has made swings of four or five pfennigs a day the norm in recent months, boosting the cost of buying options cover.

Zeneca, which works on a 12-month rolling horizon said it can spend up to 16 million pounds a year on hedging about half of its underlying foreign currency exposure, which is estimated by Russell to be worth around 1.7 billion pounds.
"I think this is a small price to pay to secure a much more flexible position," he said. ($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
